name: Xiaolingtong (小灵通)
blurb: China's cheap local "mobile" phone service on PHS, free to receive calls, 1998–2014
title: What Was Xiaolingtong (小灵通)? China's Cheap PHS Phone, 1998–2014
description: Xiaolingtong (小灵通) was China's low-cost PHS wireless phone service, launched in 1998 by landline operators, peaking in 2006 and switched off in October 2014.
answer: Xiaolingtong (roughly "little and handy") was a cheap wireless phone service in China built on Japan's PHS (Personal Handy-phone System) technology and run by landline operators as an extension of the home phone. It launched in Yuhang, Zhejiang, in January 1998, and because receiving calls was free and calls cost a fraction of mobile rates it reached about 93 million users by 2006. The government then ordered its frequencies cleared for 3G, and every base station was switched off on 1 October 2014.

body: In the late 1990s China Telecom and China Netcom held fixed-line licences, not mobile ones. Xiaolingtong let them offer something that looked like a mobile phone but was officially a wireless extension of the local landline: you got a local number, and the handset only worked inside the city where you signed up, with no national roaming.

PHS used very small, low-power cells, with a base station every two hundred metres or so. Calls dropped when you moved quickly, and coverage indoors and in tall buildings was patchy. A popular rhyme went: "Holding my xiaolingtong, standing in the wind and rain, switching from left hand to right, still can't get through."

sections.h: Why so many people used it
body: Price. When it launched in Yuhang, only the caller paid: receiving was free, the monthly fee was 20 yuan and calls cost 0.2 yuan a minute, against roughly 0.6 to 0.7 yuan on mobile networks at the time. Equipment came largely from UTStarcom and ZTE. While mobile phones were still expensive, a xiaolingtong was the first phone many people carried around.

head: Year
What happened
rows: January: Xiaolingtong launches in Yuhang, Zhejiang
Peak of about 93.4 million users in mainland China
February: regulators order the 1900–1920 MHz band cleared by the end of 2011 for TD-SCDMA 3G
About 24 million users remain and the deadline slips
1 October: all Xiaolingtong base stations are switched off

body: No. The network in mainland China is gone, and old handsets cannot make calls. Operators closed the service city by city and moved users to mobile networks. PHS has also ended in Japan, where SoftBank's Y!mobile stopped its commercial PHS service in 2023.

faq.q: Why was Xiaolingtong signal so bad?
faq.a: PHS base stations were low-power with a range of a couple of hundred metres, so coverage had gaps and calls dropped when moving quickly.

faq.q: How was it different from a mobile phone?
faq.a: It was legally a wireless landline: local number, local use only, no roaming, but much cheaper with free incoming calls.
Its 1900–1920 MHz band interfered with China Mobile's TD-SCDMA 3G network, and cheaper mobile phones were already drawing users away.
